rationale: Method: I computed a passage rate per work, count__domains__DISTANCE_TRAVEL / n_passages; every work has exactly one passage. Works dated year>=1876 count as late. Within each of the 8 genres I took an equal-weight mean over works for each period and subtracted early from late, then averaged those differences equally across genres. Point estimate: -0.0129. Uncertainty: a 1000-replicate bootstrap clustered by author (1669 authors) gives a 95% CI of [-0.042, 0.015]. A bootstrap resampling works within genre-by-period cells gives [-0.039, 0.014]. Both intervals include zero. The per-genre differences point both ways, from +0.021 for adventure to -0.066 for romance, and the small early cells (35-259 works each) make them noisy. Robustness: moving the cutoff changes the sign or leaves the estimate near zero (1860: +0.003; 1870: -0.015; 1880: -0.015; 1890: -0.018). Splitting by date confidence also gives inconsistent signs (high -0.022, medium +0.037, low -0.036), and so does splitting by origin (UK +0.010, US -0.086, unknown 0.000). Decade means rise slightly toward the 1920s, but that trend does not show up as a pre/post-1876 contrast once genre is held fixed. Coverage: 6766 works and passages from 1800 to 1925, and 92% of works fall after the cutoff, so the early estimates are imprecise. Alternative explanations for any apparent difference include changes in which genres were sampled, a few prolific authors, misdated works, the national mix of the corpus, and labeling error. Conclusion: I find no robust historical shift. The cited passage IDs are tagged with the travel/distance domain at confidence 1.0. They show what the construct looks like but say nothing about a trend.
